**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

The world you entered was still raw from catastrophe and electric with dread about what came next.

**Fourteen days before your birth — the biggest news of your birth month:** On February 6, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham, age 56. His daughter Elizabeth, 25 and mid-tour in Kenya, learned she was queen before she could get home. You were born into a Britain suspended between monarchs — the old king freshly buried, the new queen not yet crowned. Elizabeth II would reign for the next 70 years, dying in September 2022 when you were 70 years old. Her reign and your life are almost exactly congruent.

**Your exact birthday, ten years forward:** On February 20, 1962 — your tenth birthday — John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, completing three circuits aboard Friendship 7 before splashing down in the Atlantic. The space race, which had dominated your childhood, paused to celebrate on your birthday. You share that date with one of the defining moments of American ambition.

**The atomic shadow at your birth:** The United States had tested its first thermonuclear weapon — not an atomic bomb but a hydrogen bomb, orders of magnitude more destructive — in November 1951, months before your birth. The Soviet Union tested its own that same year. You were born into a world where the arsenals being assembled could end civilization, a fact your parents understood viscerally. That those arsenals would be partially dismantled before your 40th birthday, without ever being used, is perhaps the most improbable good luck of your lifetime.

**The Korean War, still grinding:** The fighting that would kill roughly 3 million people was stalemated near the 38th parallel when you arrived, deadlocked over prisoner repatriation. The armistice that ended it came in July 1953, when you were 16 months old. You grew up in a country that had fought two world wars and one major land war in Asia in the span of 40 years and was deeply uncertain whether the pattern would continue.

**Television was just becoming real:** In 1952, coast-to-coast live television broadcast had only just become possible in the United States. You are among the first generation for whom television was simply present from birth — not a novelty but a fixture. That medium would shape politics, culture, and collective memory in ways no one yet understood. Before you turned 50, a second medium of comparable power — the internet — would emerge and reshape the world again.

**The arc of your 74 years:** You were 17 when humans walked on the moon. You were 37 when the Berlin Wall fell, dissolving the defining geopolitical anxiety of your entire childhood and young adulthood in a matter of weeks. You were 49 on September 11, 2001. You watched the global population grow from roughly 2.5 billion at your birth to over 8 billion today. You have lived through the complete transformation of how human beings communicate, work, and know things — from party lines and carbon paper to smartphones and machine intelligence.

The world of February 20, 1952 — still governed by the generation that stormed beaches, still running on coal and vacuum tubes, still unsure whether the Cold War would stay cold — is barely recognizable. The person who entered it has witnessed more fundamental change per decade than any prior generation in recorded history.
